source.title: Leveraging inductive bias of neural networks for learning without explicit human annotations

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares learning on naturally noisy candidate labels with 45% randomly flipped labels and measures learning curves, training accuracy and test performance. It tests related label-noise and learning-order behavior, but does not reproduce the original experiment with a completely random labeling of the entire training set.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. for fitting random labels; that cited result is not recorded as this paper's result. Rows below cover the paper's own comparisons and measurements on candidate labels, a clean subset, and 45% randomly flipped labels. Figure-only curve values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests V6 in a new setting: naturally noisy candidate labels. Its own clean-subset and overall training measurements show clean examples being fitted before mislabeled examples. The natural-versus-synthetic noise comparison does not itself measure this learning order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but omits the main practical conclusion: early stopping on sufficiently large candidate datasets can outperform training on the original clean datasets. The authors attribute this to faster fitting of clean examples and find naturally structured noise easier to fit and less harmful than uniformly flipped labels.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses large naturally noisy candidate datasets and a 45%-uniformly-flipped comparison, rather than assigning a completely random label to every training example. It uses early stopping and compares learning curves and test performance.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports outcomes varying with candidate-label noise and dataset size, and with semantic overlap among classes. For the label-noise comparison, the type of noise (structured candidate noise versus uniformly flipped labels) changes fitting speed and the cost of overfitting.

fits_no_version.finding: At approximately matched dataset size and label-error probability, candidate data is fitted faster and overfitting harms test performance less than uniformly corrupted data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise structure affects fitting speed and the generalization cost of memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: All six Table 1 models achieve higher best test accuracy when trained on the larger candidate dataset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early stopping on sufficiently large naturally noisy datasets can outperform training on smaller clean datasets.

record.problems: The paper does not test a fully random labeling of the entire training set. The comparisons relevant to random corruption use 45% uniformly flipped labels. Several learning-rate and accuracy comparisons are described qualitatively from figures without exact values in the text. The clean subset used in the CIFAR-10 experiment corresponds to the original CIFAR-10 test set and is a subset of the candidate training set, as described by the authors.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure curves without textual numeric values are represented only where the text explicitly describes their outcome; precise values were not read from plots.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error with unchanged training settings, and chance-level test performance.
Fitting-time ratio for random versus true labels and systematic convergence slowdown with increasing random corruption.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

A random-label corruption sweep from none to all, perfect training fit throughout, and test error approaching chance. Section 4 instead substitutes naturally noisy candidate images, sometimes also changing dataset size.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and generalization after removing these regularizers.
Learning order under completely random labels; the directly separated clean/noisy evidence concerns naturally noisy candidate datasets.

missing.what: The authors explicitly state that ResNet can perfectly fit the candidate training data, including mislabeled examples. Record this later memorization endpoint alongside R2's early clean-subset advantage.
missing.locator: Section 3.2, paragraph following the early-stopping discussion; Figure 3

record.verdict_notes: The DenseNet plateau does not warrant a V6 limits_scope verdict: V6 concerns learning order, not guaranteed eventual memorization of every noisy example. The supplied plain text does not preserve readable curve trajectories, so no numerical curve values are inferred.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment assigns completely random labels to the entire training set and measures training error and chance-level test error.

The paper says candidate data is fitted faster than artificially perturbed data, but does not measure the time to fit completely random labels versus true labels or show a small constant-factor time cost, nor a systematic slowdown as random corruption rises.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs are tested.

The paper varies the proportion of clean examples replaced with candidate examples and separately compares candidate labels with 45% randomly flipped labels. It does not sweep random corruption from none to all, establish perfect training fit throughout such a sweep, or show steadily rising test error toward chance.
Weight decay, dropout and data augmentation are not evaluated as barriers to fitting random labels or as necessary conditions for generalization.

The paper compares clean and false labels in candidate datasets and shows learning curves for clean subsets, but does not report a separate test of the specific mechanism or setup in Arpit et al. (2017).
